title: Kolkata's Jhal Muri Gets Edible Paper Twist At Hyderabad's Anaganaga Restaurant
excerpt: The Jubilee Hills Telugu restaurant serves the Kolkata street snack on a sheet of edible paper, part of a menu that reworks familiar Indian dishes at a 200-cover venue built on years of culinary research.
body:
• Anaganaga, a Telugu restaurant in Hyderabad's Jubilee Hills, serves Kolkata's Jhal Muri on a sheet of edible paper that diners can eat with the snack.
  • Jhal Muri is Kolkata's spicy puffed-rice street snack, traditionally served in paper cones and finished with mustard oil and lime.
  • Anaganaga is a 200-cover restaurant developed through more than three years of research travel across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
  • The same approach runs through its menu, from dosa waffles to snacks served in edible cones.

A Kolkata street snack has been given an unusual new serving style in Hyderabad. According to NDTV Food, Anaganaga, a Telugu restaurant in Jubilee Hills, prepares its Jhal Muri on a sheet of paper and finishes it with a squeeze of lemon. The reveal, shown in a video shared by a content creator, is that the paper itself is edible: diners can eat it together with the snack or after finishing it. The creator took a bite of the paper and the Jhal Muri together and called the snack yummy, a small change that NDTV Food said left viewers surprised and curious about the dish.

Context

Jhal Muri, which literally translates to spicy puffed rice, is one of the defining street snacks of Kolkata. As Slurrp describes it, the snack is a mixture of puffed rice with fried nuts and lentils, chopped green chillies, lime juice and roasted peanuts, topped with a drizzle of flavoured mustard oil, and it is traditionally served in makeshift newspaper cones. Vendors mix the ingredients in a steel vessel with chaat masala, rock salt, chilli powder, dried mango powder, chanachur, onions, coriander and tamarind water, and each serving is customised to the customer's liking. Slurrp notes that versions of the dish are eaten as Bhel Puri in Mumbai and Churumuri in Karnataka, and that British chef Angus Denoon took the snack to London, where he set up a Jhal Muri stall and described it as a "small piece of personal theatre that you eat". Slurrp also traces the snack's Kolkata roots to Bihari workers who migrated to the city during the British Raj. Against that history, Anaganaga's version keeps the defining elements of the dish — the puffed rice, the spice and the lemon — and changes the one thing street vendors have always treated as disposable: the paper it is served on.

Impact

The edible-paper Jhal Muri fits the wider concept at Anaganaga, which mainly serves Telugu food along with dishes inspired by different parts of India, according to NDTV Food. The restaurant serves dosa waffles with avocado dip, a millet salad with yoghurt mixed with mango pickle oil and sweet tamarind, and a crispy pumpkin leaf snack topped with onion chutney instead of the usual masala papad, NDTV Food reported. It also uses edible cones made from drumstick leaves, serves churros with green and ginger chutneys and a spicy red chilli chutney, and serves Muntha Masala, a beach snack inspired by Visakhapatnam, in an edible cone made from potato starch. The restaurant behind the menu is substantial. According to Restaurant India, Anaganaga – Telugu Culinary Tales is a 200-cover premium restaurant on Road No. 45 in Jubilee Hills, spread across two floors, and launched by F&B entrepreneurs Rohith Vasireddy and Gopichand Cherukuri. Its concept was developed through more than three years of research and over 25,000 kilometres of travel across Telangana, Rayalaseema and Andhra regions, with the menu itself developed through around two years of culinary research, Restaurant India reported. The culinary programme is led by Corporate Chef DVS Pavan Kumar. Vasireddy explained the intent behind reworking familiar dishes: "The intention is not to modernise Telugu food merely for novelty, nor to preserve it behind glass. It is to understand what makes a dish what it is, retain the memory and integrity at its core, and explore how that food can continue to live across generations."

What's Next

Anaganaga is part of the Onamaalu initiative, which focuses on preserving and presenting Telugu culinary heritage through food, stories and cultural references, according to Restaurant India. The founders plan to widen the restaurant's footprint beyond Hyderabad, with expansion to Bengaluru and Visakhapatnam among the stated next steps, and a longer-term aim of reaching wider Indian and eventually international markets. For now, the edible-paper Jhal Muri is the clearest small example of that plan in action: a snack that belongs to Kolkata's streets, served in a Hyderabad dining room built to tell Telugu food stories, with the serving paper itself turned into part of the dish.
